content: The term environmental sensitivities refers to a range of adverse reactions that individuals may experience when exposed to environmental factors such as chemicals, electromagnetic radiation, or other agents at levels that are generally well-tolerated by the majority of the population. These reactions are not yet fully understood, unlike the well-documented effects of certain toxic environmental agents, such as heavy metals (e.g., lead, mercury), rock dusts (e.g., asbestos, silica), chemicals (e.g., hydrogen sulfide, dioxin), and biological agents (e.g., scorpion or snake venom). Environmental sensitivities do not represent a single, uniform condition with a universal cause. Terminology Associated with Environmental Sensitivities Various terms have been used to describe aspects of environmental sensitivities, including: A state of heightened reactivity to the environment Total allergy syndrome Toxicant-Induced Loss of Tolerance (TILT) Multiple chemical sensitivity (MCS) or hypersensitivity Chemical intolerance Gulf War syndrome/illness Idiopathic environmental intolerance Environmental illness Chemical injury or allergy Toxic injury Tight building syndrome Sick building syndrome Twentieth-century disease Chemically induced illness Chemophobia Electromagnetic hypersensitivity or intolerance Radiowave sickness Overlapping Conditions Environmental sensitivities often overlap with other medical conditions, complicating the clinical picture. Examples of such conditions include: This is critical for both treatment and research purposes. For multiple chemical sensitivity (MCS), a consensus among 34 experienced North American physicians and researchers has established the following diagnostic criteria: The condition is chronic. 3. 4. Symptoms improve or resolve when the triggering agents (incitants) are removed. 5. Reactions occur to multiple chemically unrelated substances. 6. Symptoms involve multiple organ systems. A systematic literature review has confirmed these criteria and suggested that neurological symptoms could serve as an additional diagnostic marker. These criteria have been validated in studies, including one involving 2,546 patients in Toronto, which demonstrated their ability to identify individuals most and least likely to be affected. Neurological symptoms such as heightened sense of smell, feelings of grogginess or spaciness, and difficulty concentrating were particularly indicative of MCS. A similar pattern has been observed in individuals with sensitivities to electromagnetic phenomena. Prevalence of Environmental Sensitivities Diagnostic criteria are used to identify individuals with environmental sensitivities and to estimate the proportion of the population affected. Some individuals with milder symptoms may not seek medical care, so prevalence estimates often rely on broader surveys. Canada In 2007, Statistics Canada reported that 5% of Canadians (approximately 1.2 million people) experience medically unexplained physical symptoms, including MCS, fibromyalgia, and chronic pain. The 2003 National Population Health Survey found that 2.4% of Canadians aged 12 or older, and 2.9% of those aged 30 or older, had been diagnosed with MCS. Among Canadian nurses, 3.6% reported chemical sensitivities in a 2005 survey. USA In the United States, the prevalence of doctor-diagnosed MCS ranges from 3.1% in Atlanta, Georgia, to 6.3% in California. Self-reported sensitivities to everyday chemicals are more common, with 11% of participants in a national survey and 16% in California reporting heightened sensitivity. In rural North Carolina, this figure rises to 33%. While it is unclear whether individuals with milder sensitivities are at risk of developing more severe conditions, recent studies suggest genetic and biochemical differences between affected individuals and control populations. Gender Women are disproportionately affected by environmental sensitivities. For example, a German study found that nearly twice as many women as men experienced sick building syndrome. Surveys consistently show that 60-80% of individuals diagnosed with environmental sensitivities are female. Socio-Economic Class Environmental sensitivities affect individuals across all socio-economic classes. However, population-based surveys suggest that people from lower socio-economic backgrounds are more likely to report medically unexplained symptoms. Conversely, clinic-based studies and surveys of citizens’ groups indicate that more affluent or highly educated individuals are more likely to seek medical care or self-help for these conditions. Age Environmental sensitivities can occur at any age, including in children. The prevalence of environmental sensitivities increases with age. For example, in Canada, the prevalence of medically unexplained physical symptoms rises from 1.6% in individuals aged 12-24 years to 6.9% in those aged 45-64 years. Among Canadian nurses, the prevalence of chemical sensitivities increases from 1.4% in those under 35 years to 4.8% in older age groups. Similarly, studies in Arizona found that 15% of college students and 37% of elderly participants reported heightened chemical sensitivities. This age-related increase has implications for the aging workforce and elderly care. Perception Unlike chemical triggers such as perfumes or molds, electromagnetic fields are not directly perceived by individuals. While electromagnetic sensitivities are plausible, they are poorly recognized. The prevalence of electromagnetic sensitivities is estimated to range from 1-3% of the population in various countries. Summary Environmental sensitivities encompass a range of conditions associated with specific circumstances (e.g., sick buildings), populations (e.g., veterans), chronic symptoms (e.g., pain or fatigue), or triggering factors (e.g., chemical injury or radiowave sickness). Diagnostic criteria for chemical sensitivities provide a framework for evaluating related conditions, including those linked to electromagnetic phenomena. Prevalence studies suggest that up to one-third of the population may experience some degree of environmental sensitivity, with approximately 1 million Canadians having doctor-diagnosed sensitivities. Women are affected at twice the rate of men, and prevalence increases with age. Sensitivities are associated with certain occupations and disproportionately affect lower socio-economic groups, although wealthier individuals are more likely to seek treatment.
